listing.description:
Draw pixel art, type a word in one of ten fonts, paste SVG code or drop an SVG file, and it stands up as a 3D object you can spin, light and dress in plastic, metal, glass, chrome, gold or wood.

Set its depth, smoothness and colour, choose a backdrop and an animation, and move the key light. Take a still up to 4K, transparent if you like, record a few loops as MP4 or WebM and trim them, or download the model as GLB, STL, OBJ or PLY for Blender, a game or a 3D printer.

It works without an account, and your design stays in the browser. Sign in to keep your shapes in My shapes, open them on any device, and share any one by a link that anyone can turn and copy, until you turn it off. A port of the open-source 3dsvg editor, with no build step.

apps.prompt:
Build a catalog as a Holm App Spec v1 app using only
https://holmhq.com/llms-full.txt for Holm; read sections 9–12 first. Use catalog/
with holm.json, public web/ files, api/main.js exporting
default { async fetch(request, env) }, standard Request/Response, env.holm
storage/auth and env.holm.web.fetch(request) fallback. No build step or
third-party runtime CDN; vendor fonts and any libraries with licenses.

- Define these repository conventions, not a claimed Holm store protocol:
  each top-level app has holm.json version, holm.symbol.svg (one black path,
  no strokes, 0 0 24 24) and listing/listing.json with subtitle, category,
  description, whatsNew and sample screenshots. Write a dependency-free
  Node scripts/index.mjs emitting root index.json: name/path/version,
  <app>/v<version> tag, h1 SHA-256 file fingerprint, size/count, identity,
  symbol path, listing and PROMPT text. Hash sorted app-relative paths and
  file SHA-256 values, then hash those “<hex>  <path>\n” lines and prefix
  the base64 digest with h1:. Exclude listing/ and hidden files; count README
  and PROMPT too. --check detects stale indexes or changed release tags;
  --tag creates missing tags. CI checks then tags versions on main.
- An App Store-like front page: a slideshow of the featured apps' cards
  (no controls; it holds under the mouse, and a mouse drags it),
  then all apps with search (as you type, kept in ?q=) and a list/grid
  switch below it; the grid is ruled like the facts strip (no boxes, lines
  meeting), each near-square cell the icon with its name centred under it,
  no Get and no hover zoom. Each app's own
  /apps/<app> page: icon/colour, version, size, category, license, swipeable
  screenshots, description, whatsNew with a folded version history (the
  index's history: each earlier tag's whatsNew and date), and source
  information. Keep each app's prompt in the index, but don't show it for
  now.
  Read the public repository index with synchronous env.holm.net.fetch,
  not global fetch; cache it in KV and keep the last good index on failure.
- Make it fast: the handler serves every page with the index and the viewer
  embedded, so the first paint waits on no API call (Holm serves a matching
  static file first, so don't name the shell index.html), and preload every
  module. Give each
  /apps/<app> page that app's title, description and listing/cover.png as
  its link preview (a 1200x630 card the repo draws with a script).
- Get opens a sheet remembering my peer/domain, with tabs for
  holm @<peer> app install github.com/<org>/<repo>/<app>@v<version> --host
  <host>, a clone-a-tag holm app deploy <app> --spec-v1, and an agent prompt
  following the app README.
- A /start guide, linked from a header button that stands out and the sheet, for
  someone with no node who will hand the work to a coding agent, never a
  terminal: what Holm is, why a node puts every app here one request away,
  then pick an app and where it runs (this computer, a server, an existing
  node) for a prompt to paste, what the agent asks (the licence is always
  the person's to accept), and the commands folded away. Then building from
  a prompt, what Holm gives an app, links to holmhq.com. Keep it airy.
  Beside its headline, vendor an MIT isometric line-figure kernel and draw
  an interactive figure on it: the apps ride a belt as crates from a store,
  through a gate (the fingerprint check), into a node drum; pointing slows
  the belt and names the crate's app.
- web/llms.txt for that agent: ground rules, the index, and setup, install,
  sign-in and server steps citing sections 4, 5, 8, 9 and 13 of the guide.
  The sheet's agent prompt comes first.
- Sign in through Holm. Signed-in people may rate/review once per app;
  edits wait for approval too. /admin hides apps, moderates reviews, shows
  rough daily views/Get/copy counts in KV and lets me change the tint.
  Authorize each route with documented isAppOwner()/isAppAdmin() checks.
  The guide does not document isNodeOwner()/isNodeAdmin(): do not assume
  those methods or promise node-role access for a fresh build.
- The guide does not document binary net.fetch responses: do not invent
  responseType: 'file'. Keep screenshots as public static files in web/
  until a documented, tested proxy/cache path is available; disclose that
  gap. Make light/dark mobile/desktop layouts, no sideways scrolling, and a

listing.subtitle: Decks you make with Claude, for your team
listing.description:
Make a workspace for your team, connect Claude, and ask for a deck. Claude drafts, tightens and rearranges, and every save lands in the deck you have open, on the slide you were looking at, with a note saying what changed.

Seven layouts keep every deck looking considered: a cover with a fan of what comes next, a statement with a highlighted phrase, cards, a flow, a screenshot with boxes and pins, numbers that count up, and the ask with owners and dates. There is no free canvas to make a mess on.

Edit words right on the slide, or every detail in the inspector: lists of cards and steps, links, colours, the picture, speaker notes. Drag slides into order, change a slide's layout without losing its words, and pick one of six accents for the deck. Every save is kept, so any earlier version can come back.

Invite teammates with a link. Decks and the picture library stay private to the workspace until you share one: a link that follows your latest save or stays on one version, and an embed for any website. Present with keys, swipes, notes and a clock, on a big screen or a phone, or print one slide per page.

listing.subtitle: Let people book you, no sign-up for them
listing.description:
Share one link and let people book time with you. Your page lives at your own address, like /@avery, with your photo, what you do, your website and profiles, and a link for each kind of meeting you offer, each showing the next time that's open. No account for them, no app, no back-and-forth.

Your free time lies on a strip of days, time running left to right like a video editor's timeline. Guests tap a shaded span and the meeting drops in, the length of the event; they drag it along the day and it snaps to the times that are open. If nothing suits them, they paint when they're free instead, even outside your hours, and where it meets your free time it glows. You see their times over your own week, drag the meeting to a time inside them and accept, or say no with a note.

Both of you get an email with Add to Calendar buttons for Google, Apple and Outlook. The guest can move or cancel with the link in their email. Paint your weekly hours on the same kind of strip, trimming and sliding spans like clips, even onto another day, where they trade places with what's in the way; drag a day over another and the two swap as you go. Pause a day with a switch, zoom the day in and out, and keep days off. Guests see times in their own zone, with daylight saving handled on both sides.

Insights show page views, visitors, profile clicks, bookings, time on page, where visitors came from, what they used and where they are, without cookies. Tracked links tag your page for a flyer, a newsletter or a talk, each with a QR code, and show which one brought each visit and booking. And you can run all of it from Claude: connect its MCP connector and it can change your profile, hours and event types, list meetings, answer requests and read your insights.
listing.whatsNew: Your own booking emails now carry a real invitation too, so your calendar adds each meeting by itself and drops it when it's cancelled. The emails lose their Add to Calendar buttons, which left Mail for the browser; the invite does that job.

apps.prompt:

https://holmhq.com/llms-full.txt for Holm. Read its v1 sections 9–12 and

(web.spa true), public web/ files and api/main.js exporting default
{ fetch(request, env) }, with booking and cancelling as public named
operations behind Holm's challenge and rate limits. No build step or
third-party runtime CDN; vendor Inter and Lucide icons with their licences.

- A signed-in person chooses a link (/@handle), their time zone and weekly
  hours (several ranges a day, days off), and event types (title, link,
  length, where: video link, phone, address or other; notice, how far
  ahead, start-time step, free time before and after, colour, on/off).
- Anyone opens /@handle or /@handle/event and books without an account.
  Show the host's free time on a horizontal strip of days, time running
  left to right like a video editor's timeline, in the guest's own zone
  (12- or 24-hour): tap a shaded span to drop in a meeting the length of the
  event, drag it to adjust (it snaps to open times), then name, email and
  notes. Never double-book; a taken time disappears.
- Guests may also ask for other times, even outside the host's hours: drop
  the meeting outside the shading, or paint spans of their own free time
  (trim the ends, slide them) and see where they overlap the host's. The
  host sees those spans over their own week, drags the meeting inside them
  and accepts, or declines with a note. Hosts paint their weekly hours the
  same way and drag a span onto another day, where it trades places with
  what's in its way; a day dragged over another swaps hours with it live, as
  you go. A switch pauses a day and keeps its hours. Every strip zooms:
  pinch, ctrl-scroll, or − and + with a button to fit the day.

  website and profile links with their icons, and each event type with its
  next open time. The host edits it under Profile, a tab of its own in the
  sidebar and tab bar, which saves as they type. Never a coloured stripe
  down the side of a rounded card.
- Insights for the host without cookies: views, visitors, profile clicks,
  bookings, time on page, sources, devices, places from time zones, and a
  visit-to-booking funnel. Tracked links: /@handle?ref=tag (also #ref= and
  utm_campaign) with a QR code adding &via=qr; the tag follows the guest to
  their booking, and Insights shows each link's visitors, scans and bookings. Expose the host's management (profile, hours,
  event types, meetings, requests, open times, insights) as auth "user"
  named operations, so Claude can run it all over Holm's MCP endpoint.
- The server has no Intl, so have the host's browser send its zone's UTC
  offsets for the next year and turn hours into real times on the server.
- Email both sides with env.holm.email: beautifully designed HTML (tables,
  inline styles, dark mode) plus plain text. Each booking email carries a
  calendar invite through email.send's calendar option, and no Add to
  Calendar buttons: a REQUEST to the guest with the host as organizer, and a
  REQUEST to the host named for the guest, organized by the sender address
  email.send reports and already accepted; a CANCEL to both when it's off,
  one UID per booking even when it moves. The booking page offers Google,
  Outlook.com and a hosted calendar file whose link doesn't end in .ics
  (Apple Mail offers to subscribe to those). Emailed links let the guest move
  or cancel; the host can cancel from their list. Give the host a private
  calendar feed.
- An Apple-quality UI on phone and desktop, with a fixed shell where only
  panels scroll: a round avatar button top right

  and Holm's analytics link for admins, and closes when it's tapped again;
  sheets that don't shrink as a search narrows; fine motion, quiet Web Audio
  sounds, and Inter weights that mean something. The signed-out home shows
  a booking card that plays itself: a pointer books a time, then asks for
  another. The card is an ordinary flat component set in a real CSS 3D
  scene, with its edge and shadow behind it and the pointer and result
  hovering in front, standing up as it scrolls into view and turning toward
  the mouse.
  It must open and move like a native app, with no flicker: a versioned
  service worker that serves the whole shell offline, pages drawn at once
  from the last answers kept in the browser and refreshed quietly, motion
  only for changes. Public pages end in a frosted footer: A Holm app, Source,
  Send feedback (the repo's feedback app, embed.js vendored).

  black path, no strokes, 0 0 24 24) and listing/listing.json with subtitle,

apps.name: margin
apps.title: Margin
apps.description: A writing platform for teams: workspaces, personas, quote comments, drawn covers, swappable themes and Claude as a co-writer.

listing.subtitle: A place for your team to write, with Claude on it
listing.description:
A writing platform for teams. Sign in, pick your name, and start a workspace for your team at its own address, such as /lumen. Invite the people who write with a single-use link. Each writer has a page there, like /lumen/@maya, and can keep personas: other names to write and comment under, which readers can't link back to them. One person can be in many workspaces.

Any post can have a drawn cover instead of a photo: an isometric line drawing in the workspace's style, on paper, in a flat colour or in bold blocks, that moves under your pointer. Point at a day and it lifts out of the calendar; move across a battery and the sun crosses the sky while it charges.

Readers comment the way they would in a book's margin: select any passage, add a note, and it stays highlighted for everyone, with the conversation beside it. Or respond to the whole post. Anyone signed in comments on any workspace, under the name they pick, and each workspace decides whether comments from outside its team wait for approval. Claps go up to fifty a person.

The editor is block-based like Notion, posts are Markdown underneath, and every page is rendered on the server, so it reads without JavaScript and search engines see it all. Themes are a few HTML templates and a stylesheet; each workspace picks one. Connect Claude and it can draft and publish posts as you, answer ordinary comments in your voice and leave anything sensitive for you.
listing.whatsNew: A pass over the details: headings wrap evenly, footer links are easier to tap, invites say how long they have left, comment times show the day, Claude's connector address is readable on a phone, post previews skip raw formulae, and the sample teams wear their own colours.

https://holmhq.com/llms-full.txt for Holm. Read its v1 sections 9–12 (with

  with feeds, a sitemap and social cards. They must feel instant: keep each
  rendered page until something visible changes, answer revalidations with
  a 304 before loading the rest of the app, keep Margin's own CSS and
  scripts in the browser under versioned addresses, and prefetch links on
  hover. Every footer has a small Holm mark ("A Holm app") and Send
  feedback, from this repository's feedback app. Posts are Markdown underneath, with

  then): an isometric technical line
  drawing (one projection, three line weights, flat colour, small labels) in
  the workspace's style (paper, a flat tone, or blocks), with a subject the
  writer picks, that reacts to the pointer. Save a PNG of it for link previews.
- Comments like Medium: select a passage to comment on it (keep the quote
  with its surrounding words so it re-anchors), or respond to the whole post;
  one level of replies; anyone signed in comments anywhere, as any of their
  names; each workspace shows comments at once, holds those from outside its
  team, or holds all. Claps, up to 50 per person. Link previews for posts.

  threads, and an editorial serif one with notes in the margin). Margin's
  admins add themes; each workspace picks one.

  dropped-in photos (shrunk in the browser) and short videos, autosave.

  it above the block, with a Copy button) and typeset LaTeX maths ($…$ and
  $$ blocks) on the server, so pages need no JavaScript; in the editor,
  formulae show typeset and open to edit. A price like "$5 and $10" stays
  text.

  drawing or a small photo, and a one-hour upload link the person opens on
  a phone (or Claude sends files to with curl). Keep photos at 2048 px, make
  smaller copies and a link-preview crop on first request, and give every
  photo on a page a srcset. Refuse SVG that can run code or load anything.
- Studio with a workspace switcher: posts, a comment inbox, team and invites,
  workspace settings (a logo too, also when starting one), your names and
  personas, Claude, and Margin's settings
  for its admins. MCP tools for Claude that take a workspace: write and edit
  posts, answer only ordinary comments (asking about anything sensitive),
  comment under any of your names, manage personas, start and run workspaces
  (settings, the team and its roles, invites, leaving), and work on themes. A short /llms.txt for agents.
- Sample content: two fictional teams with their own logos (made with
  holm app identity), writers, posts and comments, loaded from Studio.

  phones, a round avatar account button even when signed out, light, dark
  and auto. For this repository's store, use holm.json version,

holm @<peer> app deploy margin --spec-v1 --host <host>. Never replace an
occupied host without asking. Test as an admin, a workspace owner, an invited
writer, an outside reader and signed out, on mobile and desktop, in light and
dark. Report gaps honestly.

history.whatsNew: Code and maths read well now: fenced code is highlighted by language, with its name and a Copy button, and LaTeX formulae are typeset on the server, inline ($x^2$) or on their own lines ($$ … $$). In the editor, formulae show typeset and open to edit with a live preview, and Claude can write both straight into a post.

Claude can now add photos, drawings and short videos: an SVG drawing or a small photo straight from the conversation, or a one-hour upload link you open on your phone. Big photos are shrunk on arrival, and every page loads each photo at the size it shows, with a proper crop for link previews.

Pages now open almost at once: Margin keeps each rendered page until something changes and starts loading a link while you point at it. Claude can manage your personas and run a workspace's settings, team, roles and invites. A footer like the other Holm apps, with Send feedback, and claps that stay centred.

Margin is now a place where any team writes: a front page, workspaces with their own address, team and home page, personas readers can't link back to you, comments from anyone on any workspace, and drawn covers that move under the pointer.
Margin is here: team blogs with invites, personas, quote comments, claps, a block editor, swappable themes, and tools for Claude.

listing.description:
Claude Code runs in a VM, a container or a server with no speaker. Ralk is the tab on the machine in front of you: a chime when the build finishes, Olivia's voice when something needs you, a browser notification when you're in another window.

Connect Claude, Claude Code or ChatGPT once.
